title: Solve decimal multiplication and division problems (unit prices, metric conversions)

lesson.title: Multiply or Divide? Let the Story Tell You

steps.say: You already know how to multiply two decimals and count the places for the point, and how to divide by a decimal by rewriting it. Today we work on the one tricky part before all that: looking at a real shopping story and deciding which of the two to use.

Here is the whole secret. Ask yourself one question: does the story give me the total, or does it give me one part? If I know the total and I want one equal part, I divide. If I know one part and I want the whole total, I multiply. Look at this bar: the long bar is the total cost, and it is cut into equal one kilogram pieces.

visual.caption: Total given → divide.  One part given → multiply.

steps.say: Let's try it at the grocery store in Kamloops. A bag of apples weighs two point five kilograms and costs eight dollars and seventy-five cents altogether. What does one kilogram cost? The story gives me the total, eight seventy-five, and I want one part. So I divide. Eight point seven five divided by two point five is three point five zero. One kilogram costs three dollars and fifty cents. Check it on the bar: three fifty, plus three fifty, plus one seventy-five for the half kilogram, adds up to eight seventy-five. It fits!

Now the mistake I see most often. Blueberries cost four dollars and eighty cents per kilogram, and Nadia buys one point five kilograms. Lots of kids see the little word ‘per' and think, that word means divide, and they write four point eight divided by one point five equals three point two. But wait — three dollars and twenty cents for more than one kilogram, when one kilogram alone already costs four eighty? That is less money for more berries. That cannot be right. Here the story gives me one part, the price of one kilogram, and asks for the total. So I multiply. Four point eight times one point five is seven dollars and twenty cents. Never pick your operation from a keyword — picture the story instead.

So before you touch the numbers, whisper to yourself: total to one part means divide, one part to total means multiply. Then do the decimal work you already know, and give the answer a quick common sense sniff.

lesson.answer: Don't grab a keyword — picture the story: total → one part means divide; one part → total means multiply.

practice.question: At a craft shop in Victoria, ribbon costs two dollars and forty cents per metre. Maya buys three point five metres. How much does she pay? Careful — the word ‘per' is in there, but think about the story: are you given the total, or one part? Try drawing a bar for each metre yourself.
practice.answer: She is given one part (the price of one metre) and asked for the total, so she multiplies: two point four zero times three point five equals eight dollars and forty cents. (Check: 2.40 + 2.40 + 2.40 + 1.20 = 8.40.)
